title: Flora Hamilton
text:
I’m an environmental data scientist specializing in remote sensing and geospatial analytics in Western landscapes
Currently, I’m a Research Associate at Colorado State University’s Natural Resource Ecology Laboratory (NREL) supporting rangeland management research. My current work integrates varied datasets from field samples, remote sensing technology (drones & satellites), animal GPS data, and other sources to analyze ecological patterns and support evidence-based landscape management.
Coding/Workflow Stack: R, Python, Google Earth Engine, ArcGIS, QGIS, Remote Sensing Analysis, Machine Learning, Data Visualization, Excel, Data Management, Modelling, Git

title: Research Projects
text: My work spans remote sensing, spatial ecology, statistical modeling, and applied conservation science. Below are selected highlights of my research projects and technical publications.

title: Research Projects
text:
Research Highlights

Post-fire snowpack dynamics
2024–2026
Wildfire can reshape how snow accumulates and melts across mountain landscapes, with implications for downstream water resources. This project examines snow-depth patterns across burn severities, snow zones, and seasons in Colorado’s Front Range watersheds using airborne lidar, field observations, and terrain data. A manuscript exploring these relationships is currently in preparation.


Mapping quaking aspen after wildfire
2025–2026
Quaking aspen plays an important role in forest diversity and post-fire recovery, but its distribution can be difficult to map across large landscapes. This project combines optical satellite imagery, radar, and terrain data with random forest modeling to identify aspen occurrence in northern Colorado. Model predictions are evaluated using spatial validation and independent reference observations.


Cattle movement and rangeland use
2024–Present
How do cattle move through and use rangelands under different virtual fencing configurations? Using GPS-collar observations, this research examines livestock movement, grazing, resting, and spatial patterns of pasture use. The work explores how environmental conditions and management treatments relate to cattle behavior and landscape use.


Evaluating virtual fencing in rangelands
2024–2026
Virtual fencing offers new possibilities for managing livestock without conventional physical fences, but understanding its ecological implications requires long-term monitoring. This project synthesized four years of vegetation observations across 47 monitoring plots, using statistical analyses and climate data to examine vegetation conditions and trends associated with rangeland management.


Improving individual tree-crown mapping
2025–Present
Mapping individual tree crowns across large landscapes often requires processing imagery in overlapping tiles, which can introduce duplicate tree detections. This project develops spatial methods to identify and resolve overlapping crown polygons, improving the consistency of tree-crown datasets across the New Mexico Highlands.

title: About
text:
Curently, I’m an Ecological Research Associate at Colorado State University’s (CSU) Natural Resource and Ecology Laboratory (NREL), contributing to ecological management projects in Western landscapes, including grazelands and forests. I use data science methods, geoprogramming, and machine learning to synthesize remotely-sensed and field sampled datasets to evaluate field conditions and management impacts.
I have varied professional experiences, from working with tech startups in venture capital, leading contract projects, working for academic research institutions, to classroom teaching.
I am passionate about using data science to deepen our understanding of the natural world and translating those insights into more informed approaches for improving human interactions with natural systems.

I grew up in Taiwan and Oregon, two vastly different regions each with their unique ecosystems. Taiwan’s mountains host a range of forest types, from subtropical forests in the lowlands to temperate and alpine forests at higher elevations. On the other hand, Oregon’s high deserts, alpine forests, and basalt rock groups together create a whole other universe for exploration. My early acquaintances with these two polar opposite natural worlds — mangrove forests, banyan trees, stag beetles, blue magpies, and Formosan Rock Macaques in Taiwan— and redwoods, salmon berries, and huge Columbia Sturgeon in Oregon, fostered a life-long appreciation for productive ecosystems and the natural world.
